paragraphs: Magnetic resonance scanners collect measurements in a frequency representation called k-space. Collecting enough measurements to reconstruct a detailed image takes time, contributing to the difficulty of using MR for population-level disease surveillance. This paper studies a different acquisition objective: selecting measurements that support disease prediction directly, without first reconstructing an image.

The proposed Adaptive Sampling for MR method, ASMR, learns a policy that selects k-space samples sequentially. Its sampling decisions are adaptive and optimized for detecting a target disease. This makes the acquisition process sensitive to the prediction task, rather than treating image fidelity as the main criterion for choosing measurements.

Across eight pathology classification tasks involving knee, brain, and prostate scans, ASMR came within 2% of a fully sampled classifier on six tasks while using 8% of k-space. It also outperformed the sampling methods EMRT, LOUPE, and DPS. These results support task-directed sparse acquisition for the evaluated classification problems; the reported measurement fraction describes k-space use, rather than a directly measured reduction in total scan time.
icml-2024-adaptive-sampling-of-k-space-i.tldr: ASMR adaptively selects MR measurements for disease detection, approaching fully sampled classification performance on six of eight tasks using 8% of k-space.

paragraphs: Goal-conditioned reinforcement learning can use a graph of intermediate goals to plan a route toward a desired destination. Existing graph planners emphasize transitions that the agent can confidently complete, then apply shortest-path algorithms to connect them. The paper identifies an overlooked issue: failing to track unattainable transitions can waste repeated attempts on subgoals the agent cannot reach.

BEAG constructs a grid graph that records both achieved and unattained subgoals. The grid adaptively divides the goal space, allowing its resolution to change locally as exploration proceeds. This representation supports breadth-first exploration: the agent first probes a broad range of subgoals on a coarse grid before spending effort on detailed exploration with a denser grid.

The authors provide theoretical analysis and empirical evidence for this approach. In the complex environments they evaluate under their proposed fixed-goal setting, BEAG is the only tested approach that succeeds. The finding supports organizing exploration around both successes and unsuccessful attempts, with adaptive refinement helping determine where additional exploration effort should go.
icml-2024-breadth-first-exploration-on-a.tldr: BEAG tracks reached and unattained subgoals on an adaptive grid to prioritize broad exploration before detailed local search.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether a language model's internal activity can help predict the truthfulness of its generated text. Existing approaches based on entropy or the model's stated uncertainty can be difficult to compute, sensitive to configuration choices, or unreliable for generative tasks. The authors investigate an alternative signal inside the model.

Their method uses local intrinsic dimension, or LID, of model activations to characterize truthfulness. The central move is to examine the dimensional structure of internal representations rather than relying only on output uncertainty. This connects the assessment of generated answers to how the model represents information while producing them.

Experiments on four question-answering datasets demonstrate the method's effectiveness. The authors also investigate how intrinsic dimensions relate to model layers, autoregressive language modeling, and training. Together, these studies suggest that intrinsic dimension can be useful both for predicting truthfulness and for understanding model behavior more broadly. The empirical finding concerns a predictive signal in activations, rather than a guarantee that an individual generated answer is true.
icml-2024-characterizing-truthfulness-in.tldr: Local intrinsic dimension of internal activations provides a useful signal for predicting language-model truthfulness on four question-answering datasets.

paragraphs: Overparameterized models can be easier to optimize and generalize well, but their extra parameters increase computation. This paper investigates whether low-dimensional structure in data and training dynamics can preserve those advantages within a much smaller representation. Its theoretical starting point is deep, overparameterized low-rank matrix recovery.

For that setting, the authors show that each weight matrix's learning dynamics remain within an invariant low-dimensional subspace. This allows them to construct compact factorizations that retain the benefits of the larger parameterization. In deep matrix completion, the resulting method substantially improves training efficiency while preserving the advantages attributed to overparameterization.

The paper also introduces Deep LoRA for language-model fine-tuning, extending the existing low-rank adaptation approach. The reported benefits are less overfitting and a simpler hyperparameter setup at comparable efficiency. Experiments on natural-language tasks support its usefulness, particularly with limited fine-tuning data. The matrix-recovery theory supplies the structural motivation, while the language-model experiments establish the reported practical benefits in adaptation.
icml-2024-compressible-dynamics-in-deep-.tldr: Compressing low-dimensional training dynamics preserves overparameterization benefits in matrix learning and motivates Deep LoRA for less overfitting in language-model adaptation.

paragraphs: Contrastive learning improves representations by comparing positive examples with negative ones. Choosing negatives from a large collection becomes costly when the desired sampling distribution changes during training. In particular, a softmax distribution requires a normalization term whose computation can make sampling expensive.

EMC² uses an adaptive Metropolis-Hastings procedure to generate negatives during optimization. These samples account for how difficult the negatives are for the current model. The method targets the global contrastive objective introduced in SogCLR, pairing that objective with a sampling procedure designed to keep computation and memory costs low.

The authors prove convergence to an O(1/√T)-stationary point after T iterations, with the convergence claim holding regardless of batch-size choice. Here, global convergence refers to reaching stationarity for the global loss, rather than finding a globally optimal solution. Experiments pre-training image encoders on STL-10 and ImageNet-100 show effective small-batch training and performance comparable to or better than the tested baselines. The contribution joins a batch-size-independent stationarity guarantee with practical negative sampling.
icml-2024-emc-2-efficient-mcmc-negative-.tldr: EMC² efficiently samples difficult contrastive negatives and proves convergence to stationarity regardless of batch size.

paragraphs: Graph invariance learning aims to find features that remain useful when test data differ from training data. Existing approaches often assume something about how strongly misleading, or spurious, features correlate with labels. Those assumptions can fail when the correlations are unknown or change in real applications.

The paper introduces EQuAD, which builds on the observation that information maximization encourages learning spurious features across different correlation strengths. EQuAD uses those learned features as part of a disentangling process: tailored objectives separate invariant information from the spurious information captured through infomax. The authors provide a proof that these objectives elicit invariant features.

This approach makes learning spurious information an intermediate step toward obtaining more reliable graph representations. Experiments vary the degree of bias in synthetic data and also use challenging real-world datasets. The reported results show stable, improved performance, with gains reaching 31.76%. These findings support the proposed strategy across the tested bias conditions, addressing sensitivity to assumptions about spurious correlation strength.
icml-2024-empowering-graph-invariance-le.tldr: EQuAD learns spurious graph features through information maximization, then disentangles invariant features to improve generalization across changing biases.

paragraphs: A successful video edit needs to preserve visual detail and remain consistent as the video progresses. Diffusion-based editing systems can instead introduce blur and flicker, making the modification disrupt the original video's flow. This paper investigates a frequency-related source of that quality loss.

The authors identify high-frequency leak as a frequent cause: during denoising, the diffusion model fails to synthesize high-frequency components accurately. Their proposed Frequency Adapting Group, FRAG, introduces a receptive-field branch intended to preserve those components. It targets the denoising process itself, where the paper locates the loss of visual information.

FRAG operates without additional training and is designed to be model-agnostic. Evaluations on the TGVE and DAVIS video-editing benchmarks support improvements in consistency and fidelity. The contribution links an observed failure mode to a targeted intervention, making preservation of high-frequency components central to editing quality. Its model-agnostic, training-free design also makes the method relevant as an addition to existing diffusion editing systems.
icml-2024-frag-frequency-adapting-group-.tldr: FRAG preserves high-frequency components during diffusion denoising to improve video-editing consistency and fidelity without additional training.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization searches for good solutions when evaluating the objective is expensive. Teacher-Student Bayesian Optimization, or TSBO, aims to reduce the number of these costly labeled queries by using semi-supervised learning. It combines a teacher model, a student model, and a sampler that chooses unlabeled locations in the search space.

The teacher supplies predicted labels for the sampled locations, and the student learns from them. Feedback from the student selectively regularizes the teacher, helping it produce better pseudo labels. This interaction improves the generalization of the Gaussian-process surrogate used to guide the search.

The authors introduce two optimized sampling methods so that student feedback aligns with the optimization objective. They also use teacher-student uncertainty to make feedback more reliable when pseudo-label predictions are risky. Across several global optimization tasks with tight labeled-data budgets, TSBO substantially improves sample efficiency. Its central contribution is coordinating where synthetic supervision is produced, how it is learned, and how its uncertainty influences the teacher.
icml-2024-high-dimensional-bayesian-opti.tldr: TSBO combines optimized unlabeled sampling, teacher-generated labels, and uncertainty-aware student feedback to improve Bayesian optimization under tight evaluation budgets.

paragraphs: Generative AI offers another way to produce diverse, good-quality content across media. That changes the competitive environment for human creators and raises concerns about oversaturated markets and the marginalization of human creativity. This paper studies the tension through a formal competition model.

The authors generalize the Tullock contest to represent competition involving human creators and generative AI. They use both theory and simulations to investigate the resulting dynamics. This approach puts the relationship between the two sources of content into an explicit analytical framework, allowing the possibility of coexistence to be examined as a competitive outcome.

The analysis and simulations suggest that a stable equilibrium between human and AI-generated content is possible despite the challenges. This is a claim about a possible outcome of the model, rather than a prediction that every content market will settle into coexistence. The paper's contribution is a framework for reasoning about that possibility and the competitive interplay between human creativity and generative technology.
icml-2024-human-vs-generative-ai-in-cont.tldr: A competition model and simulations suggest that stable coexistence between human and AI-generated content is possible.

paragraphs: Small pretrained weights in language models are often treated as candidates for removal because their magnitudes suggest limited importance. This paper examines that assumption through downstream task difficulty. Its Junk DNA Hypothesis proposes that apparently minor weights can contain knowledge needed for difficult tasks.

The authors introduce metrics for comparing difficulty within a task category and across categories. Their experiments find a monotonic pattern of downstream performance degradation as more pretrained weights are removed by magnitude, revealing a relationship with task difficulty. They also report that losses on difficult tasks can remain irreparable even when downstream continual training is allowed.

The study spans different model sizes, tasks, datasets, and pruning methods. Quantization does not display the same clear monotonic effect in their evaluations, so the observed pattern does not extend equally to every compression approach. The findings challenge assessments of redundancy that ignore which tasks a model must support: weights that appear expendable under some evaluations can carry information that matters for harder downstream use.
icml-2024-junk-dna-hypothesis-pruning-sm.tldr: Experiments suggest small pretrained weights carry knowledge for difficult tasks that magnitude pruning can irreversibly damage.

paragraphs: Online continual learning trains a network on a stream whose data distribution changes over time. Experience replay mixes earlier examples into training to reduce forgetting and underfitting on past data. This paper identifies a further problem: replay-based training can follow unstable optimization trajectories that reduce overall accuracy.

The authors observe this instability even when the replay buffer contains every previous training example. That result suggests that retaining more examples alone does not resolve the issue and that it is distinct from catastrophic forgetting. Their solution, Layerwise Proximal Replay, changes the optimization geometry to make learning more stable.

LPR balances updates from new and replayed data while allowing only gradual changes to hidden activations for past examples. This constrains how quickly the model's internal treatment of earlier data can move during training. Across multiple evaluated settings, LPR consistently improves replay-based online continual learning at different replay-memory sizes. The results make stability of representation updates an additional consideration alongside the amount of past data retained.
icml-2024-layerwise-proximal-replay-a-pr.tldr: Layerwise Proximal Replay improves continual learning by stabilizing hidden representations of past examples during replay-based training.

paragraphs: Large vision-language models handle tasks that combine visual information and language, but evaluating that breadth is difficult. The paper argues that existing benchmarks cover too few tasks and emphasize basic capabilities. MMT-Bench expands evaluation to tasks requiring expert knowledge as well as careful visual recognition, localization, and reasoning.

The benchmark contains 31,325 curated multiple-choice visual questions across 32 broad task categories and 162 subtasks. Its scenarios include vehicle driving and embodied navigation. This breadth supports a task map for examining model capabilities and identifying tasks that fall inside or outside a model's domain.

The authors evaluate 20 publicly available vision-language models, including the proprietary GeminiProVision model. The results show that MMT-Bench poses substantial challenges for the evaluated systems. Its contribution is an evaluation resource for studying performance across many kinds of multimodal understanding. The task map makes the variety of abilities part of the assessment, supporting the stated goal of tracking progress toward more general-purpose multimodal models.
icml-2024-mmt-bench-a-comprehensive-mult.tldr: MMT-Bench evaluates vision-language models with 31,325 visual questions spanning 162 subtasks and reveals substantial challenges for current evaluated systems.

paragraphs: Vision Transformers capture relationships across image tokens, but standard attention becomes quadratically more expensive as token counts grow. Linear attention reduces that scaling burden, yet its cost still depends on the size of each attention head. Making heads smaller improves mobile efficiency but can weaken their ability to learn useful feature subspaces.

Mobile-Attention addresses this tradeoff with a competition mechanism between heads, supported by information flow. The mechanism reduces excessive emphasis on less useful subspaces while preserving important ones. This lets the model use small per-head dimensions while maintaining the representation capacity needed for vision tasks.

Replacing standard attention with Mobile-Attention produces models with enhanced capacity and competitive performance across several computer-vision tasks. The authors also report substantial latency reductions on the iPhone 12. These results connect the design to measured mobile execution, alongside its linear complexity in token count. The contribution is a way to make small attention heads more effective, allowing the efficiency choice to retain useful modeling capacity.
icml-2024-mobile-attention-mobile-friend.tldr: Mobile-Attention uses competition between small attention heads to improve mobile efficiency while preserving useful visual representations.

paragraphs: Learning representations of molecules in three dimensions can support downstream molecular tasks. A common approach trains an encoder to denoise atomic coordinates. Through analytical experiments, this paper identifies two problems with that setup: a mismatch between pretraining and downstream objectives, and disruption of the identifiers used to distinguish atoms.

Mol-AE addresses these problems with an auto-encoder architecture that uses positional encoding as atomic identifiers. The authors also introduce a training objective called the 3D Cloze Test. Its purpose is to help the model learn spatial relationships between atoms from real molecular substructures, giving the representation-learning process a different basis from coordinate denoising.

The proposed changes jointly address the architecture, atom identification, and training objective. Empirical results show a large performance improvement over the current state-of-the-art 3D molecular modeling approach used for comparison. The stated finding supports the combined Mol-AE design as a stronger representation-learning method, with its motivation grounded in specific weaknesses the authors identified in the prevalent pretraining framework.
icml-2024-mol-ae-auto-encoder-based-mole.tldr: Mol-AE combines an auto-encoder, positional atom identifiers, and a 3D Cloze Test objective to improve molecular representation learning.

paragraphs: Neuron shapes are important for studying brain function and neurodegenerative disorders, but collecting real morphology data is expensive. Traditional generation methods depend heavily on manually chosen rules and parameters. The learning-based MorphVAE method offers another approach, yet the paper reports that its outputs often look implausible and have invalid branching structures.

MorphGrower generates neuronal morphology in successive layers, conditioning each new layer on the structure already produced. Within a layer, it generates pairs of sibling branches synchronously. This design follows the idea of natural neuronal growth and uses the branching process itself to ensure topological validity while allowing detailed generation.

On four real-world datasets, MorphGrower substantially outperforms MorphVAE. The authors also simulate electrophysiological responses to assess whether the generated shapes are plausible from a neuroscience perspective. That additional evaluation connects morphological generation to the behavior associated with neuronal structure. The contribution combines a construction rule that guarantees valid topology with empirical evidence for greater realism and physiologically relevant plausibility.
icml-2024-morphgrower-a-synchronized-lay.tldr: MorphGrower builds neuron shapes layer by layer using synchronized sibling branches, ensuring valid topology and improving plausibility over MorphVAE.

paragraphs: Accelerated algorithms for minimax optimization and fixed-point problems have recently used an anchoring mechanism to achieve optimal convergence rates. Matching lower bounds establish that those worst-case rates cannot be improved in the relevant setting. This paper asks whether achieving that optimal rate requires the same acceleration mechanism.

The authors construct new algorithms that attain exactly the same worst-case convergence rates while using materially different mechanisms. They relate these algorithms to earlier anchor-based methods through H-duality. That relationship provides a way to obtain alternative accelerated methods without giving up the established optimal guarantee.

The resulting family of algorithms also exhibits different empirical characteristics. This matters because equality of worst-case rates does not imply identical behavior in actual runs. The paper establishes non-uniqueness of optimal acceleration and opens a route to studying alternatives within the same theoretical performance class. Its contribution is the existence and construction of different optimal mechanisms, alongside evidence that those differences can matter empirically.
icml-2024-optimal-acceleration-for-minim.tldr: H-dual algorithms achieve the same optimal worst-case rates as anchor-based methods through different acceleration mechanisms.

paragraphs: Pruning removes model weights to make large language models easier to deploy. Many existing methods apply the same sparsity level to every layer. This paper investigates whether the distribution of unusually large token features, called outliers, can guide a more effective allocation of sparsity across layers.

The authors analyze token-feature distributions and identify a strong relationship involving outliers. They propose Outlier Weighed Layerwise sparsity, or OWL, which assigns non-uniform sparsity ratios based on each layer's outlier ratio. As described in the abstract, the assigned sparsity ratio is directly proportional to that outlier ratio. The method therefore makes layerwise feature statistics part of the pruning decision.

Evaluations cover LLaMA-V1/V2, Vicuna, OPT, and Mistral across multiple benchmarks. At 70% sparsity, the paper reports perplexity improvements of 61.22 over Wanda and 6.80 over SparseGPT, alongside a 2.6× end-to-end inference speedup in DeepSparse. These results support adapting sparsity across layers and demonstrate a deployment benefit in the stated inference engine.
icml-2024-outlier-weighed-layerwise-spar.tldr: OWL uses layerwise feature-outlier ratios to allocate non-uniform sparsity, improving heavily pruned language models and reporting faster DeepSparse inference.

paragraphs: Proteins adopt multiple conformations, and understanding that range of shapes is important for understanding their functions. Physics-based methods such as molecular dynamics face difficulties sampling rare events and reaching equilibrium. Diffusion models offer a generative alternative, but existing score-based methods can produce conformations that deviate substantially from the equilibrium distribution.

The paper attributes this problem to inadequate incorporation of physical prior knowledge. Its proposed method, ConfDiff, is a force-guided SE(3) diffusion model that combines a force-guided network with a mixture of data-based score models. This brings physical guidance into a generation process that also draws on learned structural information.

ConfDiff is designed to produce diverse conformations while retaining high fidelity. Experiments include conformation prediction tasks for 12 fast-folding proteins and Bovine Pancreatic Trypsin Inhibitor, or BPTI, where it outperforms the state-of-the-art method used for comparison. The results support combining force guidance with learned scores to improve conformation generation across the evaluated protein tasks.
icml-2024-protein-conformation-generatio.tldr: ConfDiff combines physical force guidance with learned diffusion scores to generate diverse, high-fidelity protein conformations.

paragraphs: This paper studies how multiple learning agents can acquire new abilities through interaction while preserving their existing expertise. Its motivating analogy is socialized learning in human cultural evolution, where collective intelligence supports learning. The target goes beyond simply adding new classes: performance on original expert classes is explicitly prioritized.

The proposed Multi-Agent Socialized Collaboration framework, MASC, draws inspiration from population genetics and cognitive science. It includes collective collaboration and reciprocal altruism modules that organize collaboration, share information, and support knowledge exchange among agents. These mechanisms aim to let agents learn new classes while maintaining the stated directional advantage on their original areas of expertise.

An extensive empirical study demonstrates the effectiveness of multi-agent collaboration for this objective. The central contribution is a learning setup and framework that treat continued specialization and acquisition of new abilities as linked goals. Information exchange is therefore organized around making agents better learners while preserving the importance of the expert knowledge they already hold.
icml-2024-socialized-learning-making-eac.tldr: MASC organizes multi-agent knowledge sharing to learn new classes while prioritizing agents' original expertise.

paragraphs: Spiking neural networks attract interest for their efficiency and accuracy, and conversion from conventional artificial neural networks is one route to building them. Existing conversion methods have matched conventional-network accuracy with low latency in convolutional vision models. Transformer-based spiking models, however, have continued to lag behind their conventional counterparts in accuracy.

SpikeZIP-TF introduces a conversion method specifically for Transformer-based networks. The authors claim exact equivalence between the artificial and spiking networks produced by their method, so conversion incurs no accuracy degradation. This directly addresses the accuracy gap that motivates the work, making preservation of the original network's behavior central to the conversion.

The converted models achieve 83.82% accuracy on ImageNet and 93.79% on SST-2, exceeding the state-of-the-art Transformer-based spiking networks used for comparison. The evaluations cover both computer vision and natural-language processing. Together, the equivalence claim and reported results support conversion as a route to accurate spiking Transformers across these two task domains.
icml-2024-spikezip-tf-conversion-is-all-.tldr: SpikeZIP-TF converts Transformers into exactly equivalent spiking networks without accuracy loss and reports strong vision and language results.

paragraphs: This paper identifies two limitations in decoder-only Transformers that combine causal masking with relative position encoding. First, softmax attention forces some weight onto attended tokens even when the current embedding already contains sufficient information. Second, limited representation of absolute position prevents the studied relative-position Transformers from being universal approximators.

StableMask addresses both issues by changing the causal mask without adding parameters. It introduces pseudo-attention values to balance attention distributions and uses a progressively decreasing mask ratio to encode absolute positional information. The mask thus helps control both how attention is distributed and what positional information the model can represent.

The authors support the method with theoretical analysis and empirical evaluation. They report significant improvements across language models ranging from 71 million to 1.4 billion parameters, using varied datasets and encoding methods. StableMask also integrates with existing optimization techniques. The contribution shows how a change to masking can address representational and attention-allocation issues within the decoder-only architecture.
icml-2024-stablemask-refining-causal-mas.tldr: StableMask modifies causal masking without extra parameters to improve attention allocation and encode absolute position.

paragraphs: Model-based reinforcement learning learns how an environment transitions between states. This paper studies what happens when an adversary corrupts those dynamics. Robust regression techniques used in model-free reinforcement learning do not transfer directly, so the authors develop methods based on maximum likelihood estimation of the transition model.

For online learning, corruption-robust optimistic MLE, or CR-OMLE, weights estimation using uncertainty measures based on total-variation information ratios. Its regret bound scales as √T + C up to suppressed factors, where T is the number of episodes and C is cumulative corruption. A matching lower-bound argument establishes that the additive dependence on corruption is optimal.

For offline learning, the authors adapt the weighting strategy into corruption-robust pessimistic MLE, CR-PMLE. Under a uniform coverage condition, corruption worsens suboptimality by O(C/n), nearly matching the lower bound. The two algorithms give provable robustness guarantees for learning transition models in both settings, with the offline result explicitly depending on adequate coverage in the available data.
icml-2024-towards-robust-model-based-rei.tldr: Uncertainty-weighted maximum likelihood yields corruption-robust model-based reinforcement learning with provable online and conditional offline guarantees.

paragraphs: Evidential deep learning estimates uncertainty, but the paper identifies weaknesses in detecting unfamiliar inputs and in classification. Its diagnosis separates two causes: uncertainty does not adequately reflect a test example's distance from training data, and the conventional parameterization of concentration parameters limits classification performance.

Density Aware Evidential Deep Learning, or DAEDL, addresses both causes. At prediction time, it combines the evidential model's output with the test example's density in feature space. It also introduces a new parameterization to resolve the problems attributed to the conventional one. The method therefore changes both the information used to assess uncertainty and the way evidential outputs are parameterized.

The authors prove favorable theoretical properties and report state-of-the-art results across a range of uncertainty-estimation and classification tasks. The findings support incorporating feature-space density into evidential predictions. They also show the value of addressing classification and out-of-distribution detection together through changes targeted at the distinct weaknesses identified in the original approach.
icml-2024-uncertainty-estimation-by-dens.tldr: DAEDL combines feature-space density with a revised evidential parameterization to improve uncertainty estimation and classification.

paragraphs: Dataset distillation creates a small synthetic dataset that retains useful information from a larger real dataset. Models trained on these compact datasets can perform well, but that success leaves open what the synthetic examples actually encode. This paper investigates their behavior, representativeness, and the information carried by individual examples.

The study finds that distilled data cannot replace real training data outside the standard dataset-distillation evaluation setting. It also identifies a mechanism behind retained task performance: distillation compresses information associated with the early training dynamics of models trained on real data. This connects the usefulness of distilled examples to the learning process they reproduce.

The authors additionally provide an interpretation framework and show that individual distilled points contain meaningful semantic information. Together, the findings describe distilled data as carrying both training-related information and interpretable content. They clarify why strong performance in the standard evaluation setting does not establish general interchangeability with real data, while explaining some of the information that enables compact synthetic datasets to work.
icml-2024-what-is-dataset-distillation-l.tldr: Distilled datasets encode early training dynamics and meaningful semantics, but do not generally substitute for real data outside standard distillation evaluation.

paragraphs: Autoregressive language models face two efficiency bottlenecks: attention costs grow quadratically with token count, and generation proceeds sequentially. Linear attention and speculative decoding offer ways to address these problems, but their combined effectiveness is uncertain. This paper studies existing linear-attention methods in autoregressive models and their integration with speculative decoding.

The authors introduce an augmentation to linear attention that makes it compatible with speculative decoding. The aim is to improve both training and serving efficiency while retaining effective language modeling. Their evaluation includes seven existing linear-attention models and five encoder- or decoder-based language models, together with ablation studies examining the proposed approach.

The experiments consistently support the augmented linearized models. Compared with prior linear-attention methods, the approach reports up to a 6.67 reduction in perplexity on LLaMA and up to a twofold generation speedup. These are maximum reported improvements, rather than gains claimed for every configuration. The contribution connects changes to attention with decoding strategy to improve both prediction quality and generation efficiency.
icml-2024-when-linear-attention-meets-au.tldr: Augmenting linear attention for compatibility with speculative decoding improves language-model quality and yields up to twofold generation speedups over prior linear-attention methods.
